ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Reduction in holidays 
*241.   SHRI LALITBHAI MEHTA: † 
 SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: 
Will the Minister of PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCS AND 
PENSIONS be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of days a year, the Government of India employees work 
considering holidays of Saturdays, Su ndays, Gazetted Holidays, Restricted 
Holidays and various types of leave availed by them; 
(b) whether Government have examined the possibility of reducing the 
Gazetted Holidays by permitting employ ees of respective religious faiths a 
holiday on that particular day and avoid closing of Government offices; 
(c) whether Government have also examined the possibility of restoring a six day 
week to increase the number of working days; and 
(d) whether Government propose to conduct any study on the effects of 
observance of so many holidays on developmental works and routine 
administration of Government of India? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI HARIN PATHAK): (a) to (d) 
A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Lalitbhai Mehtra. 

RAJYA  SABHA [6 August, 2003] 
Statement 
(a) So far as Central Government Administrative Offices covered by 
the Five day week system are con cerned, employees avail themselves 
of Saturdays and Sundays (about 104 in a year), two Restricted Holidays 
and 17 Gazetted Holidays (out of which normally 3-4 holidays fall on 
Saturdays and Sundays, thereby reduc ing the effective holidays to an 
average of 14 per year). 
Those Central Government employees who are governed by the Central Civil 
Services (Leave) Rules, 1972 are entitled to 30 days Earned Leave, 20 days Half Pay 
Leave and 8 days Casual Leave (for admini strative offices) per year.These are, 
however, personal to the employees and are availed by them as per their 
requirement, subject to sanction of  the leave, based on administrative 
exigencies. Earned Leave if not availed during the year may be carried forward 
subject to a ceiling of 300 days, Half Pay Leave if not availed during the year 
may be carried forward without any limit. Casual Leave and Restricted Holidays 
cannot, however, be carried forward if not availed within the Calendar year. 
Therefore, the number of days in a year the Government of India employees work 
vary depending upon the number of days of leave availed by him/her during the 
year. The maximum number of days Central Government administrative offices 
remain open in a year is about 247 days. 
Other than the Central Government offices functioning on five day week 
basis a large number of Central Government organisations, including Industrial and 
Operational Organisations function on six day week basis keeping in view their 
operational requirements. In fact some organisations related with delivery of 
essential services, work round the clock. Therefore, the number of days 
Government employees work in these units, in a year, is essentially dependent on 
the nature of functions being performed by these units, and the regulations 
governing the hours of work and leave in those units. 
(b) It is not desirable to restrict employees to avail themselves holidays based 
on religious faiths only. 
(c) Consequent to the Fifth Pay Commission Recommendations, the issue 
pertaining to re-introduction of the six day week working was reexamined. It 
was, however, decided to continue the five day week'system in Central 
Government Administrative Offices. 
(d) The report of the 5th CPC and 2nd National Labour Commission,

the same have been utilised?

RAJYA SABHA [6 August, 2003] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL): (a) to (c) A statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Under the Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY), some of the States/UTs are not 
sending Monthly Progress Reports regularly. 
(b) The Central assistance under the scheme is released every year to the 
District Rural Development Agencies (DRDAs) in two instalments, subject to 
the fulfillment of the following conditions. 
(i) The first instalment amounting to 50% of the Central allocation for a 
particular DRDA is released in the beginning of the financial year, if 
second instalment during the previous year was claimed and released 
without any condition. 
(ii) The second instalment of funds for the district is released on receipt of 
request from the DRDAs in the pres cribed proforma alongwith Audit 
Report/UC of previous year etc. after utilising 60% of total available 
funds including opening balance and State share etc. 
(iii) Central share to the tune of 3/4 times of the amount exceeding 
permissible opening balance in the district (i.e. 15% of the district 
allocation of the previous year) is deducted from the amount of 
second instalment. 
(iv) The graded cut from 10% to 30% of Central allocation is imposed on 
the quantum of second instalment if complete proposal is received late 
(from January to March of the financial year). 
All this is to ensure that the funds allotted to the States under the Scheme 
are being utilised and are not being reappropriated for other purposes. 
(c) State-wise details of amount allocated, released and utilised under the 
Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY) during 2002-03 are annexed as Statement-I.

System to forewarn people about cyclones 
*259.   MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that  in the last cyclone there was 
heavy loss of life and property as the residents of the coastal areas could not 
be forewarned well before time; 
(b) if so, whether Government have now developed any system to 
forewarn the people before such a natural calamity takes on them; and 
(c) if so, the success of such a system and how far it has been used to 
save the lives and property of coastal people? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SWAMI CHINMAYANAND): (a) In the Orissa Super-Cyclone of 
1999, there was heavy loss of life and property not on account of a lack of 
forewarning but due to the intensity of the cyclone, heavy storm surge and 
continuous down pour. 
(b) and (c) The cyclonic systems both in the Bay of Bengal and the 
Arabian Sea are being monitored and tracked by the India Meteorological 
Department (IMD) through a chain of high power coastal radars, high wind speed 
recorders and a network of surface and upper air observatories 
51 

RAJYA  SABHA [6 August, 2003] 
along the coastline. India's present capability is such that no cyclone 
approaching the Indian coast can escape detection and the information is made 
available through the INSAT based Cyclonic Warning Dissemination Systems and 
radio and TV channels both at the national and regional levels. The technology 
upgradation of the monitoring systems is also a continuing process at the 
IMD.The cyclone tracking and warning systems have proved to be effective. 
Cyclone alerts and warnings are bein g communicated to the States well in 
time.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (SHRl 
PRAHLAD SINGH PATEL): (a) and (b) In order to attract Foreign 
67 

RAJYA SABHA [6 August, 2003] 
Direct Investment in coal sector the Government have decided that the private 
Indian companies setting up or operating power projects as well as coal or 
lignite mines for captive consumption in such projects may be allowed foreign 
equity upto 100% provided that the coal or lignite produced by them is meant 
entirely for captive consumption in power generation. 
100% foreign investment in the equity of an Indian subsidiary of a 
foreign company or in the equity of an Indian company for setting up of coal 
processing plants in India may be allowed subject to the conditions that such an 
Indian subsidiary or the Indian company (a) shall not do coal mining and (b) 
shall not sell the washed coal or sized coal from their Coal Processing Plants 
in the open market and shall supply the washed coal or sized coal from their 
Coal Processing Plants to the respective parties sending raw coal to such Coal 
Processing Plants for washing or sizing. 
The other private Indian companies engaged in exploration or mining of 
coal and lignite for captive consumption for production of iron and steel and 
production of cement may be allowed foreign equity upto 74%. 
The Government has liberalized its Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) policy 
in the mining sector which allows foreign equity holding upto 100%, on the 
automatic route for all non-fuel and non-atomic minerals except diamonds 
and precious stones, This covers exploration, mining, mineral processing and 
metallurgy. In the case of diamonds and precious stones, foreign equity upto 74% 
is allowed on the automatic route for both exploration and mining operations. 
However, proposals seeking higher than 74% foreign equity for diamonds & 
precious stones are considered by the Foreign Investment Promotion Board 
(FIPB).The Mines & Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act, 1957 has also 
been suitably amended to make it more investor friendly. 
(c) and (d) Keeping in view the recommendations of the Committee on 
Integrated Coal Policy (Chari Committee), the Central Government decided in 
February, 1997, among other things, to set up an Independent Body to perform the 
functions of monitoring and processing the proposals for exploration of coal and 
lignite in the country and allotment of new coal and lignite blocks to Indian

Details of Welfare Measures for Defence Personnel and their Families 
Medical 
There is a good network of hospitals for the serving personnel. All 
military hospitals attend to day to day medical requirements of servicemen and 
their families. 
Specialized Medical Treatment 
(a) Research and Referral Hospital: For serving soldiers requiring 
specialized medical treatment, a supe r specialist hospital is available 
at New Delhi. 
(b) Paraplegis Rehabilitation Centres (PRCS)-.Two PRCs, At Kirkee and 
Mohali are available for rehabilitation of disabled soldiers. 
(c) St. Dunstan's After Care Organisation: This organisation provides 
training to the visually handicapped servicemen at the national 
Institute for visually handicapped at Dehradun. 
(d) Artificial Limb Centre (ALC): One ALC is available at Pune for 
providing of artificial limbs to disabled soldiers. 
2. Now, a medical scheme called Ex-servicemen Contributory Health 
Scheme (ECHS) has been approved, which caters for comprehensive medical 
cover to the ex-servicemen in receipt  of any kind of pension including 
disability pension and family pensioners, spouse as also 
80 

[6 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
legitimate children and wholly dependent parents.The scheme envisages to 
establish 104 augmented medical inspection rooms at military stations and 123 
new poly clinics at non military stations.The scheme contributory in nature has 
commenced w.e.f. 1st April 2003 and would be fully implemented by March 
2008. 
3. For the time being till ECHS becomes operational, service hospitals 
would continue with entitled treatment and AGI's extended Medical Benefit 
Scheme (MBS) and financial assistance for AG's Welfare Fund and KSB 
for medical treatment would also continue. 
Financial Assistance 
4. Financial assistance is granted to the ex-servicemen, widows and 
their dependent family members from Raksha Mantri's Discretionary Fund 
(RMDF) and AG's Welfare Fund for assistance to old, infirm, for marriage 
of daughters, repair of houses, medical treatment etc. 
Education 
5. In order to provide quality education to the children of army personnel 
posted deployed in far flung areas, 116 army schools have been 
established. Besides, the Air Force have established 148 schools in most 
of the units to provide educational facilities to the children of air force 
personnel and the Navy has establishe d 9 Naval Public Schools. 7 schools 
have been established by Air Force Wives Welfare Association for mentally 
and physically challenged children. 
Educational concessions 
6. Children of defence personnel killed or permanently disabled in action 
who are studying in institutions under the department of Education are granted 
complete exemption from tuition fee and other fee levied by the institution. 
7. Educational scholarships are awarded by the Army, the Navy and the Air 
Force to the wards of serving soldiers, based on both merit and means. 
8. 28 seats in MBBS, 1 seat in BDS, 2 seats in Engineering in 
Annamalai University and 2 seats each in the 7 IITs (subject to qualifying 
81 

RAJYA SABHA [6 August, 2003] 
the Joint Entrance Examination) are available for the wards of servicemen and ex-
servicemen. 
Vocational Training 
9. The three service Headquarters make arrangement for Vocational 
Training to their respective servicemen at various civil institutions, prior to 
their retirement, for their post retirement settlement. 
Housing 
10. Army Welfare Housing Organisation provides limited no. of houses to 
servicemen and ex-servicemen in select stations at reasonable costs. Similar 
housing facilities are provided by Air Force Naval Housing Board to Air Force 
and Naval personnel. 
11. Various State Governments have made reservations for serving/ retired 
defence personnel/dependents in allotment of house sites/houses. 
12. 37 War Memorial Hostels have been constructed to provide 
accommodation to wards of war bereaved and disabled personnel to enable 
them to pursue their studies. 
Transit Facilities 
13. Over 252 Sainik Aram Grahs have been established at many stations 
where servicemen have to transit while being on duty or proceeding to/returning 
from leave. Besides, 15 holiday homes have also been established at select 
stations. 
14. Journey by air is provided to serv icemen and their families while 
travelling on duty or leave to and from Leh sector in J&K. 
15.75% concession in rail fare and airfare in Indian Airlines domestic flights 
is provided to recipients of certain gallantry award winners and to widows of 
posthumous winners of the gallantry awards along with a companion. 
Canteen Facilities 
16. Items of daily needs are provided at concessional rates to servicemen 
and their families through the Canteen Stores Department and the Unit Run 
Canteens.

Ranganadi Hydro Electric Dam 
1879. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether discharge of water from Ranganadi Hydro Electric Dam 
through Dikrong River of Assam has taken place; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the ac tion contemplated to take up flood 
protection measures of Dikrong River as part of the total project? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Yes, Sir.The transfer of water from 
Ranganadi Hydro Electric Project to th e Dikrong River has taken place since 
the commissioning of Ranganadi H.E. Project in January, 2002. 
(b) The water conductor system of the project has been designed for a peak 
discharge of 160 cumecs.The actual discharge, into Dikrong River, however, 
depends on the generation at Ranganadi Power House. In lean season, only 1 unit 
of the project can be run at 65 MW continuously which would discharge about 26 
cumes of water to Dikrong River. 
Due to additional maximum discharge of 160 cumecs in monsoon 
months, rise of water level in different stretches of the Dikrong River in Assam 
portion would range from 7cm. to 12 cm. At Banderdewa, the rise would be 7 
cm. and at Sissapathar the same will be 12 cm. The observed peak flow of 
Dikrong River at Sissapathar bridge is 2500 cumes (upto 1997). The 
incremental discharge of 160 cumecs is very insignificant in comparison. 
The flood protection work of the downstream reaches of Dikrong river 
beyond Banderdewa Bridge as existing (without transfer of 160 cumecs of 
water from Ranganadi basin to Dikrong basin) is not sufficient to retain the 
observed 2500 cumecs discharge of river Dikrong during the peak flood 
season. No embankment has so far been constructed by the 
134 

[6 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
State   Government to cater to observed 2500 cumecs of discharge peak flood 
to protect the population. 
Keeping this in view, NEEPCO has decided to keep the power house 
under shutdown during such peak floods  and no additional water would be 
discharged to Dikrong River during flood season.

1889. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the objective of the national housing policy to end 
shelterlessness by the Ninth Plan ha s been achieved; if so, the details 
thereof; 
(b) the number of housing units built up so far against the target fixed for 
the purpose; 
(c) what are the hurdles experienced in achieving the targets; and 
(d) what steps are being contemplated for successful implementation of 
National Housing Corporation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M. K. PATIL): (a) to (d) The Central 
Government announced in 1998 a National Housing and Habitat Policy which 
aims at providing 'Housing for AH'. Pursuant to the National Housing Policy, 
special Action Plan was prepared for construction of additional 13 lakh new 
houses annually in the rural areas in addition to the existing target of about 
12.50 lakh houses annually with an emphasis on extending benefits to the poor 
and the deprived. During the last three years of the 9th Five Plan period, against 
the target of 75.90 lakh, around 52.38 lakh houses have been constructed under 
the Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY) and thr ough HUDCO & National Housing 
Bank (NHB). One of the major constraints in implementation of the Action 
Plan is inadequate budgetary resources. As a result, shelterlessness in rural 
areas by the end of 9th Plan could not be achieved in full.

Jute mills in the country 
1918. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) how many jute mills were there in the country upto December, 1997; 
(b) how many of these jute-mills are existence till 31st March, 2003; 
(c) whether any new jute-mill has been set up during this period; 
(d) the reason why these mills are getting sick year to year; and 
(e) the steps towards modernisation of this category of mills? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI BASANAGOUDA R. PATIL): (a) There were 73 jute mills in the 
country upto December, 1997. 
(b) There were 78 jute mills in the country as on 31st March, 2003. 
(c) During this period three new composite jute mills in Andhra Pradesh 
and two composite mills in West Bengal have been set up. 
(d) Out of 78 jute mills, 37 jute mills are sick at present. It has generally 
been noticed that certain  common factors with regional variations have 
mainly been responsible for the indus trial sickness of these mills. These 
factors are instability in production of raw jute, high labour cost, demand 
erosion due to emergence of jute substitute products, obsolete machinery, lack

On the implementation of Conditional Access System and criteria for 
uplinking for foreign channels 
Ǜी संजय िनरुपम (महाराÍटर्): महोदय, मȅ आपके  माध्यम से सूचना और Ģसारण मंतर्ी का 
ध्यान कं डीशनल एक्सेस िसÎटम को लागू करने का फै सला और अपिंलिंकग के  िलए फॉरेन चैनल का 
जा कर्ाइटेिरया है, उसकी ओर आकिर्षत करता हूं। 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING (SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): Hon'ble 
Chairperson, Shri Sanjay Nirupam and other Members have drawn my 
attention to the implementation of Conditional Access System (CAS), and also 
the criteria for uplinking policy for foreign channels. Let me inform this hon'ble 
House about the decisions taken by the Government. I would like to make a 
brief statement on the issues raised by the hon. Members in their notices. 
The genesis of this exercise lies in  the fact that having mandated the 
Conditional Access System through an amendment in the Cable Television 
Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, and the prevalent confusion and chaos and 
uncertainties regarding rates and lack of  transparency in the system, it was 
necessary that the consumers be protec ted from this arbitrariness and a 
scientific rational approach be adopted for working out the rates of free-to-air 
channels in the basic service tier. 
As the hon. Members are aware, t he Government had set up a 'Task 
Force' comprising the various stakeholders like Cable Operators' Association,    
Multi-System   Operators   (MSOs),   Broadcasters,   Consumer 
180 

[6 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Electronics and T.V. Manufacturers ' Association (CETMA) besides the 
Consumer Groups and Technical Expert s to examine the various issues 
related to and oversee the implementation of the Conditional Access System 
(CAS) as provided under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 
1995. 
The Cost Accounts Branch (CAB) of the Ministry of Finance was also 
requested to commission a study and the effort was to get a feedback from 
the cable operators on important issues. Several meetings were also held 
where they were invited to give their suggestions/comments. The C.A.B. .had 
detailed discussions with the technical experts, including equipment 
manufacturers, Broadcast Engineering Consultants India Ltd. (BECIL), etc. 
Pursuant to the recommendations  of this Task Force, the 
Government, through a notification issued on 14 th January, 2003, notified the 
introduction of C.A.S. with effect from 15 th July, 2003, in the four metros., and 
through a notification issued on 7 th May specified the minimum number of 
free-to-air channels to be included in the package of channels forming the 
basic service tier to be Rs.30 and the maximum amount which a cable 
operator can demand from a subscriber to  be Rs.72. I may also point out that 
the few Multi System Operators have alre ady assured that they will be able to 
show between 60 to 70 free-to-air channels within the maximum cost of 
Rs.72/-. 
I. FOLLOW-UP ACTION BY THE MINISTRY 
I would like to assure the" hon. members that there has been no 
confusion in the implement ation of C.A.S. On the contrary, the Government 
has taken a number of initiatives for its smooth implementat ion in the four 
metres. I would like to inform the House that the Government has been in 
constant and continuous dialogue with the representatives of stakeholders in 
the industry, i.e. manufacturers, broadcasters, MSOs and cable operators. 
The present state of pr eparedness indicated that adequate Set Top Boxes 
were not likely to be available by the deadline, i.e., 15th July, 2003. Hence, 
the Government has deferred the im plementation of the CAS to 1st 
September, 2003 and proposes to im plement it in a phased zone-wise 
manner in the three metres of Delhi, Kolkata and Mumbai. As far as possible, 
these zones have been carved out with distinctive features in order 
181 

RAJYA SABHA [6 August, 2003] 
to provide minimum overlap of the services between zones of each city. As far 
as Chennai is concerned, based on the feed-back from the MSOs in Chennai, 
it has been decided to implement it at one go. 
The intervening period will be used to step up preparedness, build 
up consumer awareness and enable the im portation/manufacture of boxes in 
greater volumes. 
The Ministry of Finance has also reduced the customs duty from 
50.8 per cent to 5 per cent which ha s been extended until 30th September, 
2003 through its Notification dated 29th  July, 2003. It has been estimated that 
analogue Set Top Boxes would cost about Rs. 2,500/- and digital Set Top 
Boxes would cost between Rs. 2,700/- and Rs. 3,000/-. A few MSOs have also 
offered attractive introductory offers and easy affordable schemes through hire 
purchase, loan schemes, instalment basis, refundable deposit with a nominal 
daily rental, etc. As on 31.7.2003, 1,07,882 Set Top Boxes have been 
imported -- this is on the basis of the information given by the Customs 
Department. It is also expected t hat with the increasing demand and 
indigenous production and supply, the prices are likely to fall further. Steps are 
also being taken to ensure quality of the Set Top Boxes through random 
sample testing of the boxes of different  manufacturers. Visits are being made 
to head-ends to assess the level of upgradation and preparedness. All this is 
aimed at making it consumer-friendly. 
Now,  I would like to discuss the criteria on uplinking policy for foreign 
channels. 
II. UPLINKING POLICY 
The uplinking policy has been gradually developing over a span of 
five years. 
(i) In June 1998, the Cabinet, fo r the first time, permitted Indian 
satellite channels (with Indian equity not less than 80 per cent 
and effective management control in the hands of resident 
Indians) to uplink from India through VSNL only. 
182 

[6 August, 2003) RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) In March 1999, the Cabinet permitted all Indian companies (who 
were broadcasters and were as defined above) to uplink from 
India without being mandated to go through VSNL only. 
(iii)   In July 2000, the Cabinet approved the following: 
(a) Setting up of hubs/teleports by companies incorporated in 
India with not more than 49 per  cent foreigrt equity holding, 
including from NRI, OCB and PIO.

Commission, on the subject of foreign nationals as owners of

Taking note of such concerns, a note was taken to Cabinet in March, 
2003 for considering "imposition of  restrictions on ownership and 
management control of TV channels, telecasting news and current affairs 
programmes, as it was felt that these concerns had not been adequately 
addressed in the existing policy on uplinking of TV channels from India. The 
arguments given in favour of restrict ions were that a foreign owned and

While the last concern was equally applicable to all the foreign 
content telecasting channels, other concer ns were valid largely in respect of 
News and Current Affairs channels only. The potential for mischief against 
safety and security of the State was acknowledged to be more with a channel 
which is largely dedicated to News and Current Affairs' programmes than with 
other channels. 
The Cabinet vide its decision of I8 th March, 2003 inter alia approved 
foreign ownership/management control restrictions to be placed on channels 
having any element of News and Current Affairs' content and allowed to uplink 
from India. The guidelines, issued on 26th March, 2003, laid down the 
following eligibility criteria for a company uplinking News and Current Affairs 
channels including, inter alia, the following : 
(a) To be registered/incorporated in India under the Companies Act, 
1956. 
(b) Foreign equity holding in the applicant company not to exceed 
26 per cent of the total paid up capital. 
(c) Majority of its Board of Directors to be Resident Indians. 
(d) CEO of the applicant company, known by any designation, 
and/or Head of the channel to be Resident India. 
(e) News Editor (s) or authority(ies) exercising editorial control over 
news and current affairs programme(s) of the channel(s) to be 
Resident Indians. 
Throughout the evolution of the upli nking policy in stages, ownership 
and management control to vest in Indian hands has remained a prime 
concern. This was sought to be addr essed categorically in March, 2003, 
particularly, in relation to News and Current Affairs' channels. Further, by an 
order of July 15, 2003, an inter-Ministerial Group has been set up to examine 
the foreign exchange norms/guidelines, particularly, relating to uplinking of 
news and current affairs channels. The case of one of the application seeking 
uplinking as per extant guidelines is under examination.

of implementation. 
Madam, let me begin with the observation of the hon. Member, Shri

has raised a very relevant point. The Economic Times does a survey; and, on 
entertainment, they have written a very exhaustive story. The book is here

crores. By the year 2005, it is goi ng to become worth Rs.32,000 crores. The 
rate of growth is 31 per cent. Therefor e, this is one of the fastest growing 
service sectors in the country. We need to understand it. Our esteemed friend,

them. In the year 1991, by their enterprise, they brought cable into our homes.

concerned, I think, Mr. Panda has alre ady shared them wit h the House. But 
certain interesting developments are equally important. In this whole progress 
and speed of development, the consumers have taken a back-seat. You 
asked me the question as to what had be en the nature of rise in the channel 
rates. You must understand one thing. As  of now, the consumer does not 
know, how much he is paying for what. A particular book is shown to him;

some specific information. The rate of one particular pay-channel, which was

as to what has been the experience in the other countries, and, Madam, this is

rise has been only three times.   That is

vigilance includes Government rules and procedures that are internal to the /
